reachable: Yes, and it gets gradient. The objective is the module the harness calls every step; WANTS_CTX = True is picked up at harness.py:77 and the three-argument call at harness.py:100 fires, with ctx["cmd"] = stream.extract_cmd_input(b)[m] = the raw z_cmd token, shape [n, 768], aligned with pred/tgt (verified: baseline_interleave.extract_cmd_input returns batch["tok"][:, 0::2] and M.collate puts z_cmd there). The no-ctx and shift-is-None fallbacks are dead in practice: n ~ 1900 rows per batch (bs=64 sequences x ~29 steps), pool per parity ~950 >= 8, stride = 1, and the ridge solve succeeded on every batch I tried. A full 3-step _train on the real genome runs to completion on CPU (ok=True). The mechanism therefore influences every gradient the model receives, including at the cups read rows: the candidate's realized gradient share on cups/cvar read rows is 0.82-0.89 early and mid. On the arch side, r23's forward is bit-identical to r22 at init (max diff 0.0) and only tp_out receives gradient at step 1 (7.7e-4 / 8.6e-4 at the scored unpaired read); the upstream address/pointer/gate parameters get zero gradient until tp_out leaves zero, which is ordinary zero-init behavior and is disclosed in §5 as a possible non-firing mode. Reachability at the scored read is not in doubt for the objective; it is conditional for the arch's copy path, exactly as the hypothesis says.
solves_outside_model: No. Three independent checks. (1) Containment: the fitted shift exists only inside loss(); it is subtracted from pred and from tgt to form pres/tres, both fresh tensors, and the function returns a scalar. Nothing is written back to b["tok"], to the target, or to any model input, and no scoring path imports this module — the probe/CA instruments never call the objective. (2) Structure: shift_i = rho * (basis_i @ W), a linear map of row i's own command embedding plus a bias, with W shared across every row in the same parity half. It has no per-row degree of freedom, so it cannot carry "which content is at final_loc". Measured directly: over 7179 same-parity row pairs whose command strings are identical but whose targets differ (mean max-abs difference 2.609), max|shift_i - shift_j| = 0.000e+00 exactly. A quantity that resolved the move chain would have had to differ there. (3) Optimum: the diagonal distance is algebraically untouched (verified numerically, below), so the loss's attractor for row i is still t_i, the ordinary supervision target; the shift only moves where the repulsors sit. No command string is parsed anywhere in the impl — there is no string handling in the module at all, only tensor ops on the frozen embeddings. This is nothing like the retracted stream that stamped a Python-resolved content identity into the read token.
summary:
The mechanical claims are all true, and I could confirm every one of them on real embeddings rather than the author's synthetic. Diagonal invariance holds (max |d_raw(i,i) - d_res(i,i)| = 1.2e-4 on distances of magnitude ~1500, relative 8e-8). Cross-fitting is genuine: adding 100.0 to tgt[i] changes fitted[i] by exactly 0 while moving other rows by up to 14. The ridge is the dual-form linear kernel ridge described, with lambda = 0.1 * mean(diag(gram)). The "mean off-diagonal ~ 2" calibration is right on the nose (measured 2.020), so at rho=0 the relative temperature/lam/margin/tau/dup reproduce the parent's absolute constants to three digits. "Numerically-equal targets are pooled" is exactly true: the approximate class (tt_raw <= 1e-3 * mean_raw) equals the bitwise-identical class for all 1897 rows, with zero pooled-but-distinct pairs and a comfortable gap (min nonzero off-diagonal 1.6e-7 vs threshold 2.0e-3). Anti-collapse holds (constant 11.44 vs perfect 0.379). The cost ratio matches the claim (86ms vs 36ms fwd+bwd at n=1897, against the author's 59/25 at n=1600), and a full step costs +24% end to end on CPU. Nothing is computed outside the model.

What does not hold is the mechanism's stated effect, which is the whole reason the candidate exists. The hypothesis says the orthogonalization collapses window-mates so the loss must discriminate them on the canary; measured on real data, window-mate canary pairs are the least-collapsed group (0.687 of raw distance) while cross-format pairs collapse to 0.371 and the batch mean is 0.512 — so window-mates end up relatively FARTHER apart and the ring drifts off them. Downstream, the share of an anchor's repulsion aimed at other canary-content reads roughly halves versus the parent at every operating point I tested (mid: 0.251 vs 0.667), and the share aimed at its own window-mates does not move. The reason is structural and should have been visible from the author's own algebra: a linear map of a command can explain the format difference between two observations, never the random canary, so it contracts the pairs the design wanted left apart. Section 3's coupling argument — that this is what makes the r23 pointer-copy path worth opening its gate — rests entirely on that inverted effect.

The half of the design that does fire is the anchor reweighting, which is largely the imported r22 equivalence quotient rather than the new FWL step: gradient share on cups/cvar read rows goes 0.51 -> 0.89 at mid-training and empty-observation rows drop from 0.013 to 0.002. That reweighting is genuine and could well move the score. But because the hypothesis claims (incorrectly) that at rho -> 0 the objective degenerates to the parent, a positive result would be misattributed to the orthogonalization when the rho=0 loss actually sits within 1.5% of the archived r22_exact_target_equivalence_quotient and 26% away from the parent.

Caveats on what I could not check: everything is measured on frozen embeddings at hand-constructed operating points (pred = a*tgt + noise), never inside real training with a converging r23 net, so I cannot rule out that the ring geometry looks different once tp_out opens and predictions concentrate. I could not run the real GPU lane, so the score and the reported band are unknown to me, and with a 0.0227 noise floor a small movement either way would be unreadable regardless. I also did not verify the r23 arch beyond its zero-init claim; it is a pre-existing chunk and its own review is not mine.

divergences.claim: §2: 'Two window-mates whose observations differ mainly because they are cats of two different paths become a near-collapsed pair; the loss can only separate them on the command-UNEXPLAINED remainder, which is the canary content.' §3: 'nearly all of the listwise gradient is about the one thing the trunk structurally cannot supply and the pointer-copy path structurally can: which earlier observation is the right one to reproduce.'
divergences.what_the_code_does: The orthogonalization contracts the WRONG pairs. Window-mate canary pairs are the LEAST collapsed group in the batch, while cross-format pairs collapse about twice as hard, so the ring and the softmax negatives move AWAY from the content-vs-content discrimination, not onto it. This is structural, not a tuning accident: a linear map of the command embedding can explain format/type differences between two observations but cannot explain a random canary string, so exactly the pairs the hypothesis wanted collapsed are the ones it cannot collapse.
divergences.evidence: Real train embeddings (data/dockerfs3-cupsF-treat-nocwd, standardized, 64-sequence batch, n=1897 rows), pred at a mid-training operating point. Contraction ratio d_res/d_raw: window-mate canary-read pairs 0.687; cross-window canary-read pairs 0.702; canary-read vs system-read pairs 0.371; batch mean over all pairs from canary anchors 0.512. Relative to the batch mean, window-mates get 1.34x FARTHER, so exp(-tt/lam) gives them less weight. Negative posterior mass from canary-read anchors directed at other canary-content reads, parent vs candidate: early 0.252 -> 0.121, mid 0.667 -> 0.251, late 0.889 -> 0.567. Mass directed at the anchor's own window-mates: 0.0154 -> 0.0152, 0.0150 -> 0.0147, 0.0279 -> 0.0265 (flat to slightly down). Pairwise direction check: pairs with cos(t_i-t_j, s_i-s_j) in [0.7,1.0] contract to 0.259 of raw distance (hard negatives), pairs with cos in [0.1,0.3) stay at 1.008 — hardness rises with the EXPLAINED share of the difference.

divergences.claim: §2: 'On the raw standardized scale (mean off-diagonal ~ 2) these fractions reproduce the parent's 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.25 exactly, so in the rho -> 0 limit the objective degenerates to the parent's.'
divergences.what_the_code_does: The scale-fraction half of this is exactly right, but the objective at rho=0 is not the parent. The exact-target equivalence quotient (multi-positive logsumexp numerator, log_class candidate suppression, inverse-class-size anchor mass) and the energy anchor gate are unconditional — they run at rho=0 too. At rho=0 the loss reproduces the ARCHIVED r22_exact_target_equivalence_quotient, a different prior mechanism, not the parent r12. This matters for attribution: a reader who takes the sentence at face value will credit any score movement to the FWL orthogonalization, when on this data most of the measurable behavior change comes from the r22-derived quotient the candidate also imported.
divergences.evidence: Same real batch, mid operating point: candidate with _RHO=0 -> 3.976; r22_exact_target_equivalence_quotient -> 3.917 (1.5% apart); parent r12_antiretrieval_ring_negatives -> 5.368 (26% apart); candidate at _RHO=0.9 -> 3.565. Separately, the scale claim itself checks out: measured mean_raw (precision-weighted target-target off-diagonal) = 2.020, so at rho=0 temp=0.2525, lam=1.010, margin=0.505, tau=0.2525, dup_scale=0.0505 against the parent's 0.25 / 0.5*mean_raw=1.010 / 0.5 / 0.25 / 0.05.

divergences.claim: Module DESCRIPTION: 'an in-batch negative is made hard exactly to the extent that the difference between its observation and the anchor's is NOT explained by the difference between their two commands.'
divergences.what_the_code_does: Inverted. d_res(i,j) = ||(t_i - t_j) - (s_i - s_j)||^2 IS the unexplained part of the difference, and a SMALL distance is what makes a negative hard, so hardness rises with the EXPLAINED share. The body of hypothesis §2 states this correctly ('become a near-collapsed pair'); only the archived one-line DESCRIPTION has the sign backwards, and that DESCRIPTION is what future briefs surface as a PRIOR MECHANISM.
divergences.evidence: Algebra in the impl (lines forming pres/tres then dist2), plus the cos-binned contraction table above: high-cos (well-explained) pairs contract to 0.259 of their raw distance, low-cos (unexplained) pairs stay at ~1.0.

divergences.claim: §2: 'ctx["cmd"] ... so this is a per-row function of causal inputs only'.
divergences.what_the_code_does: shift_i is a per-row linear function of row i's own command, but the coefficient matrix is estimated from the opposite-parity half of the batch, which contains later steps of the same trajectory and other trajectories. It is not a function of row i's causal inputs alone. This is not a leakage defect — the shift never enters any model input, and it is provably command-determined — but the phrasing overstates the isolation.
divergences.evidence: harness.py:99 passes ctx = {'cmd': stream.extract_cmd_input(b)[m], ...}; _crossfit_nuisance fits on pool = rows of the opposite parity and applies to apply_idx. Verified the shift is nonetheless answer-independent: over 7179 same-parity row pairs sharing an identical command string but with targets differing by mean max-abs 2.609, max|shift_i - shift_j| = 0.000e+00 exactly.

divergences.claim: §2 third bullet: 'Rows are weighted as anchors by energy_i ... In this data that reallocates the contrastive budget away from the "mv -> empty output" mass and onto the expose/test reads.'
divergences.what_the_code_does: The reallocation is real and measurable, but the energy gate contributes only about a 2x tilt; the inverse-class-size factor (r22-derived, class size 613 for the empty-observation rows) does essentially all of it. And relative to the parent the realized gradient reallocation is large early/mid and vanishes by convergence, because the parent's duplicate mass already self-cancels.
divergences.evidence: Energy gate alone: mean row_w mv 0.354 vs cat 0.704. After the inv_class factor and normalization: mv share of total anchor weight 0.000, cat 0.917, ls 0.083. Realized per-row |dL/dpred| share on empty-observation rows (mv and cvar redirect), parent -> candidate: early 0.048 -> 0.001, mid 0.013 -> 0.002, late 0.008 -> 0.006; on cups/cvar read rows: early 0.554 -> 0.821, mid 0.506 -> 0.884, late 0.834 -> 0.830. Reproduced on three disjoint 64-sequence batches with the same numbers to within 0.01.
